# Hands-on: from a count matrix to cell types {#sec-workshop}

In 2h30, we go from the count matrix described in @sec-10x to a map of the
adult human testis with a name on every population, and to a first
differential expression analysis. Every step adds something to **one object**,
a `SingleCellExperiment`, which grows as we go (@fig-workflow).

![The standard Bioconductor single-cell workflow, in two parts separated by a
break.](figures/workflow.svg){#fig-workflow width=100%}

| Time | Section | Duration |
|---|---|---|
| 0:00 | [Setup](#sec-setup) | 5 min |
| 0:05 | [Reading the count matrix](#sec-read) | 10 min |
| 0:15 | [The `SingleCellExperiment`](#sec-sce) | 15 min |
| 0:30 | [Quality control](#sec-qc) | 15 min |
| 0:45 | [Normalisation](#sec-norm) | 10 min |
| 0:55 | [Feature selection](#sec-hvg) | 5 min |
| 1:00 | [Dimensionality reduction](#sec-dimred) | 10 min |
| 1:10 | [Batch effects](#sec-batch) | 10 min |
| 1:20 | ☕ [Break, and checkpoint](#sec-checkpoint) | 10 min |
| 1:30 | [Clustering](#sec-clustering) | 15 min |
| 1:45 | [Marker genes](#sec-markers) | 15 min |
| 2:00 | [Annotation with a reference](#sec-annotation) | 10 min |
| 2:10 | [Pseudobulk differential expression](#sec-pseudobulk) | 15 min |
| 2:25 | [Wrap-up](#sec-wrap-up) | 5 min |

::: {.callout-tip icon='true'}

## How to follow a live-coding session

- **Type the code, do not paste it.** You will remember a function because your
  fingers typed it. Typos are part of the lesson: you will see the error
  message, and learn what it means.
- **Say when you are stuck, straight away.** A helper will come while the
  session goes on.
- **If you fall behind, stop typing and watch.** It is better to see the next
  step than to be stuck on the previous one: at the break, a checkpoint object
  gets everyone back on track (@sec-checkpoint).

:::

## Setup {#sec-setup}

In RStudio, open a new R script (*File* > *New File* > *R Script*) and save it,
as `workshop.R` for instance. Type the code of the session in it, and run each
line with {{< kbd mac=Cmd-Enter win=Ctrl-Enter linux=Ctrl-Enter >}}.

We load the packages as we need them. Here they are, and what they are for:

| Package | Used for |
|---|---|
| `BiocFileCache` | downloading the data once, and re-using it afterwards |
| `Matrix` | sparse matrices |
| `SingleCellExperiment` | the container for single-cell data |
| `scrapper` | QC, normalisation, feature selection, PCA, UMAP, batch correction, clustering, marker genes, pseudobulk |
| `scater`, `ggplot2`, `patchwork` | plots |
| `SingleR` | annotation against a reference |
| `DESeq2` | differential expression |

They are all installed in the workshop environment. To check that they are
installed on your own computer, type `library(scrapper)`: an error means that
the package is missing.

## Reading the count matrix {#sec-read}

### Downloading the data, once

The count matrix of @guo2018 is a gzipped text file on GEO. `BiocFileCache`
downloads a file the first time you ask for it, and simply returns the path to
its local copy afterwards. In the workshop environment, the file is already in
the cache: asking for it costs nothing. (The URL is the only line of the day
worth copy-pasting.)

```{r}
#| label: get-path
library(BiocFileCache)
bfc <- BiocFileCache(ask = FALSE)
umi_url <- "https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/series/GSE112nnn/GSE112013/suppl/GSE112013_Combined_UMI_table.txt.gz"
umi_path <- bfcrpath(bfc, umi_url)
umi_path
```

### Reading it into R

The file is a table with one row per gene and one column per cell. It is big:
reading it takes about a minute.

```{r}
#| label: read-table
umi <- read.delim(umi_path, header = TRUE, row.names = 1)
dim(umi)
umi[1:5, 1:3]
```

A `data.frame` is not the right container for numbers that all have the same
type: turn it into a matrix.

```{r}
#| label: to-matrix
counts_dense <- as.matrix(umi)
class(counts_dense)
format(object.size(counts_dense), units = "MB")
```

### Making it sparse

This matrix stores every single zero. A **sparse** matrix only stores the
non-zero entries, and their positions:

```{r}
#| label: sparse
library(Matrix)
counts_sparse <- Matrix(counts_dense, sparse = TRUE)
class(counts_sparse)
format(object.size(counts_sparse), units = "MB")
```

What fraction of the entries is not zero?

```{r}
#| label: sparsity
nnzero(counts_sparse) / length(counts_sparse)
```

Only about 1 entry in 10. We no longer need the dense copies: remove them, and
let R give the memory back.

```{r}
#| label: cleanup
rm(umi, counts_dense)
invisible(gc())
```

::: {.callout-note icon='true'}

## With your own 10x data

Cell Ranger's `filtered_feature_bc_matrix/` folder (@sec-cellranger) is already
sparse: `DropletUtils::read10xCounts()` reads it straight into a
`SingleCellExperiment`, the object we build next.

:::

## The `SingleCellExperiment` {#sec-sce}

![Anatomy of a `SingleCellExperiment`.](figures/sce.svg){#fig-sce width=100%}

A matrix of counts is not enough: we will need to keep information about every
cell (donor, quality metrics, cluster...) and every gene (is it variable?),
plus several transformed versions of the matrix and low-dimensional
embeddings, without ever mixing up their rows and columns.

Bioconductor's answer is the `SummarizedExperiment`, the container used for
bulk RNA-seq: one or more matrices (the *assays*) of genes × samples, a table
describing the rows (`rowData()`), and a table describing the columns
(`colData()`), locked together. A **`SingleCellExperiment` is a
`SummarizedExperiment` whose columns are cells**, with a few extra slots for
single-cell analysis, such as `reducedDims()` for embeddings (@fig-sce).

```{r}
#| label: build-sce
library(SingleCellExperiment)
sce <- SingleCellExperiment(assays = list(counts = counts_sparse))
sce
```

Read that printout: it is the map of the object. Each slot has its accessor:

```{r}
#| label: sce-accessors
dim(sce)
assayNames(sce)
counts(sce)[1:5, 1:3]
head(rownames(sce))
head(colnames(sce), 3)
```

### Cell metadata is hiding in the column names

`colData(sce)` is empty for now. We have no sample sheet, but the name of each
cell tells us where it comes from: `Donor2.AAACCTGGTGCCTTGG.1` is the cell with
the 16-nt barcode `AAACCTGGTGCCTTGG` (@sec-gems), from replicate `1` of
`Donor2`. Split the names on the dots, and keep each piece:

```{r}
#| label: split-names
split_names <- strsplit(colnames(sce), "\\.")
split_names[1:2]
```

`$` adds a column to `colData()`, exactly as it adds a column to a data frame:

```{r}
#| label: coldata
sce$Donor <- sapply(split_names, function(x) x[1])
sce$Barcode <- sapply(split_names, function(x) x[2])
sce$Replicate <- sapply(split_names, function(x) x[3])
sce$Sample <- paste(sce$Donor, sce$Replicate, sep = "_rep")
colData(sce)
table(sce$Donor, sce$Replicate)
```

Three donors, two 10x runs each: **six libraries**, for **three biological
replicates**. Keep that in mind: it makes all the difference in
@sec-pseudobulk.

### Subsetting keeps everything in sync

`[` subsets a `SingleCellExperiment` like a matrix, `[genes, cells]`, and
subsets every slot accordingly:

```{r}
#| label: subset
sce_donor1 <- sce[, sce$Donor == "Donor1"]
dim(sce_donor1)
table(sce_donor1$Donor)
counts(sce[c("PRM1", "SOX9"), 1:4])
```

:::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note icon='true'}

#### Question

How many cells does each **sample** contribute? Which sample is the largest?

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

#### Answer

```{r}
#| label: answer-sample-sizes
table(sce$Sample)
```

:::
::::

## Quality control {#sec-qc}

Not every column of the matrix is a healthy cell (@sec-count-matrix). Some
barcodes are droplets that only caught ambient RNA, some are cells that were
damaged or dying, some are two cells captured together. We remove the worst of
them **first**, as they would distort every later step.

Three metrics are computed for each cell:

| Metric | Low-quality cells have | Because |
|---|---|---|
| total UMI count (`sum`) | few | little RNA was captured |
| number of detected genes (`detected`) | few | same reason |
| proportion of counts from mitochondrial genes | many | a damaged cell loses its cytoplasmic mRNA, while the transcripts inside the mitochondria stay behind |

### Computing the metrics

Mitochondrial genes are recognisable by their symbol, which starts with `MT-`:

```{r}
#| label: mito
is_mito <- grepl("^MT-", rownames(sce))
sum(is_mito)
rownames(sce)[is_mito]
```

`quickRnaQc.se()` computes the three metrics, stores them in `colData()`, and
flags outlier cells: a cell is an outlier when one of its metrics sits more
than 3 *median absolute deviations* (MADs) away from the median, on the bad
side (too few counts or genes, too many mitochondrial counts). Our six
libraries were sequenced to different depths, so the thresholds are computed
within each library, with `block =`.

```{r}
#| label: qc
library(scrapper)
sce <- quickRnaQc.se(
    sce,
    subsets = list(Mito = is_mito),
    block = sce$Sample
)
colData(sce)
```

The thresholds used for each library are stored in `metadata()`:

```{r}
#| label: qc-thresholds
metadata(sce)$qc$thresholds
```

and `keep` says which cells pass:

```{r}
#| label: qc-keep
table(sce$Sample, sce$keep)
```

### Look before you filter

Always plot what you are about to throw away:

```{r}
#| label: qc-plots
#| fig-height: 7
library(scater)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
p_sum <- plotColData(sce, x = "Sample", y = "sum", colour_by = "keep") +
    scale_y_log10()
p_mito <- plotColData(
    sce, x = "Sample", y = "subset.proportion.Mito", colour_by = "keep"
)
p_sum / p_mito
```

`/` stacks two plots with `patchwork`. Notice the ceilings: no cell has more
than 20% of mitochondrial counts, nor fewer than about
`r format(signif(min(sce$sum), 2), big.mark = ",")` UMIs. The authors filtered
the table before depositing it, which is common: always check what was done to
the data you download.

:::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note icon='true'}

#### Question

Not a single cell of `Donor1` is discarded. Why? Is it good news?

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

#### Answer

Look at the thresholds on the mitochondrial proportion, in %:

```{r}
#| label: answer-mito-thresholds
round(100 * metadata(sce)$qc$thresholds$subset.proportion$Mito)
```

The cells of `Donor1` have more mitochondrial counts overall: the median and
the MAD of its libraries are higher, and so is their threshold, above the 20%
ceiling of the table. None of its cells is far enough from its own median to
be flagged.

Thresholds computed within each library are **relative**: they assume that
most cells of each library are fine, and adapt to each of them. A cell with
15% of mitochondrial counts is thus discarded from `Donor2` and `Donor3`, but
kept in `Donor1`. A fixed threshold, say `sce$subset.proportion.Mito < 0.1`,
would treat all libraries the same. Neither choice is right in general: make
it knowingly, and look at the plots.

:::
::::

Let's filter:

```{r}
#| label: qc-filter
sce <- sce[, sce$keep]
dim(sce)
```

We keep `r format(ncol(sce), big.mark = ",")` cells.

::: {.callout-note icon='true'}

## Going further: doublets and ambient RNA

Two more filters are often applied, which we skip today for lack of time:
**doublets** can be found with `scDblFinder` [@germain2021], and the
contamination by **ambient RNA** can be estimated and removed with `decontX`
or `SoupX`.

:::

## Normalisation {#sec-norm}

Two cells can have different total counts for biological reasons (one is
bigger, or more active) or technical ones (one was captured, reverse-transcribed
or sequenced more efficiently). Normalisation removes the technical part, so
that expression values can be compared between cells.

The simplest approach divides the counts of each cell by a **size factor**
proportional to its library size, its total UMI count. The normalised values
are then log-transformed: a pseudo-count of 1 avoids taking the log of zero,
and the log turns fold changes into differences, so that a few very highly
expressed genes do not dominate everything else.

```{r}
#| label: normalise
sce <- normalizeRnaCounts.se(
    sce,
    size.factors = sce$sum,
    block = sce$Sample
)
summary(sce$sizeFactor)
assayNames(sce)
```

With `block = sce$Sample`, the size factors also account for the six libraries
having been sequenced to different depths. `logcounts` holds
$\log_2(\text{count} / \text{size factor} + 1)$:

```{r}
#| label: logcounts
logcounts(sce)[c("PRM1", "SOX9", "ACTA2"), 1:3]
```

From now on, everything about **expression** uses `logcounts`; everything
about **counts**, such as differential expression (@sec-pseudobulk), goes back
to `counts`.

::: {.callout-note icon='true'}

## Going further: composition bias

When cell types express very different sets of genes, library size factors are
slightly biased: this is *composition bias*. It rarely changes the clusters,
but `scran`'s deconvolution method corrects it [@lun2016]: compute the size
factors with `scuttle::pooledSizeFactors(sce, clusters = scran::quickCluster(sce))`,
and pass them to `normalizeRnaCounts.se(size.factors = ...)`.

:::

## Feature selection {#sec-hvg}

Of the `r format(nrow(sce), big.mark = ",")` genes, most are not expressed at
all, or expressed at similar levels in every cell. They carry no information
about which cell is which, but add noise to every comparison between cells. We
keep the **highly variable genes** (HVGs): those whose variance across cells is
much larger than expected for a gene of the same average expression.

```{r}
#| label: hvg
sce <- chooseRnaHvgs.se(sce, block = sce$Sample, top = 2000)
rowData(sce)
sum(rowData(sce)$hvg)
```

`rowData()` now holds, for each gene, its mean and variance of expression, the
variance expected from the trend fitted to all genes (`fitted`), the excess
over that trend (`residuals`), and whether it is one of the 2,000 HVGs:

```{r}
#| label: hvg-plot
gene_stats <- as.data.frame(rowData(sce))
ggplot(gene_stats, aes(x = means, y = variances, colour = hvg)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.5) +
    geom_line(aes(y = fitted), colour = "dodgerblue", linewidth = 1) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey70", `TRUE` = "firebrick")) +
    labs(x = "Mean of log-expression", y = "Variance of log-expression") +
    theme_bw()
```

The genes furthest above the trend:

```{r}
#| label: hvg-top
top_hvgs <- rownames(gene_stats)[order(gene_stats$residuals, decreasing = TRUE)]
head(top_hvgs, 20)
```

**Recognise anything?** `TNP1`, `PRM1` and `PRM2` (transition protein and
protamines), `HMGB4` and `LELP1` are expressed late in spermatogenesis, while
`PTGDS`, `IGFBP7` or `DCN` come from somatic cells: feature selection has found
the main axes of variation of a testis without being told anything about
testes.

## Dimensionality reduction {#sec-dimred}

### PCA

2,000 genes are still 2,000 dimensions. A principal component analysis (PCA)
compresses them into a few dozen components that capture most of the
structure. Since biology is concentrated in the first components while noise
is spread evenly across all of them, PCA also *denoises* the data.

```{r}
#| label: pca
sce <- runPca.se(sce, features = rowData(sce)$hvg, number = 25)
reducedDimNames(sce)
dim(reducedDim(sce, "PCA"))
```

How much of the variance does each component explain?

```{r}
#| label: pca-variance
pca_info <- metadata(sce)$PCA
percent_var <- 100 * pca_info$variance.explained / pca_info$total.variance
pca_df <- data.frame(PC = seq_along(percent_var), percent = percent_var)
ggplot(pca_df, aes(x = PC, y = percent)) +
    geom_col() +
    labs(x = "Principal component", y = "Variance explained (%)") +
    theme_bw()
```

The first components carry most of the signal, and we keep 25, `scrapper`'s
default: anything between 10 and 50 would give a similar picture here.

```{r}
#| label: pca-plot
plotReducedDim(sce, "PCA", colour_by = "Donor")
```

### UMAP

The first two PCs only show part of the structure. UMAP [@mcinnes2018] squeezes
all 25 PCs into two dimensions that we can look at:

```{r}
#| label: umap
sce <- runUmap.se(sce)
plotReducedDim(sce, "UMAP", colour_by = "Donor")
```

::: {.callout-important icon='true'}

## A UMAP is a picture, not a measurement

UMAP keeps cells that are close in the PCA space close in the picture, but
distances between distant groups, and the size of a group, mean little. Use it
to look at the data, and run the analysis itself on the PCs.

:::

## Batch effects {#sec-batch}

**Do the donors overlap, or does each of them form its own island?** That is
the first thing to look at, every time. Here, several populations split by
donor. Part of that is biology (donors are different people) and part is
technical: their samples were collected and processed separately. If we
cluster now, some clusters will be donors rather than cell types.

The mutual nearest neighbours (MNN) method [@haghverdi2018] pairs cells across
donors that are each other's closest match: such pairs are assumed to be the
same cell type, and the differences between them measure the batch effect,
which is then removed from all cells. `correctMnn.se()` stores the corrected
PCs as a new reduced dimension, `MNN`:

```{r}
#| label: mnn
sce <- correctMnn.se(sce, block = sce$Donor)
reducedDimNames(sce)
sce <- runUmap.se(sce, reddim.type = "MNN", output.name = "UMAP_MNN")
plotReducedDim(sce, "UMAP_MNN", colour_by = "Donor")
```

### Is any of this real?

Before trusting a picture, check it against something you know (@fig-testis):
`UTF1` marks spermatogonial stem cells, `SYCP3` meiotic spermatocytes, `PRM2`
spermatids, and `ACTA2` the peritubular myoid cells, a somatic population.

```{r}
#| label: umap-markers
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 8
plotReducedDim(sce, "UMAP_MNN", colour_by = "UTF1") +
    plotReducedDim(sce, "UMAP_MNN", colour_by = "SYCP3") +
    plotReducedDim(sce, "UMAP_MNN", colour_by = "PRM2") +
    plotReducedDim(sce, "UMAP_MNN", colour_by = "ACTA2")
```

The germ cells line up along one continuous path, from stem cells to
spermatids: the **trajectory** of spermatogenesis. The somatic cells form
separate islands.

::: {.callout-important icon='true'}

## Corrected values are for maps and clusters only

Batch correction changes the data to make donors look alike. Use the corrected
space to visualise and cluster the cells, never to test for differential
expression: for that, we go back to the raw counts and model the donor
explicitly (@sec-pseudobulk).

:::

## ☕ Break, and checkpoint {#sec-checkpoint}

Look at everything the object now holds:

```{r}
#| label: checkpoint-sce
sce
```

Two assays, quality metrics and size factors in `colData()`, gene statistics in
`rowData()`, and four reduced dimensions: one hour of work in a single
variable.

::: {.callout-tip icon='true'}

## Fallen behind? Start again from here

The workshop package holds a copy of `sce` as it is at this point, without
the `logcounts` to keep it small. Restart R (*Session* > *Restart R*), then
load it and compute the `logcounts` again, as in @sec-norm:

```{r}
#| label: checkpoint-load
#| eval: false
library(SingleCellExperiment)
library(scrapper)
library(scater)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
sce <- GenE2scRNAseqIntro::sce_checkpoint
sce <- normalizeRnaCounts.se(sce, size.factors = sce$sum, block = sce$Sample)
```

:::

## Clustering {#sec-clustering}

In bulk RNA-seq, you **know** your groups: treated and untreated, tumour and
normal. In single-cell RNA-seq, the groups are what you are looking for.

The standard approach is **graph-based clustering**:

1. connect each cell to its nearest neighbours in the (corrected) PCA space;
2. weight each connection by the number of neighbours the two cells share;
3. cut the graph into communities of densely connected cells, with a
   community-detection algorithm (Louvain, Leiden...).

It scales to millions of cells and makes no assumption about the shape of the
clusters.

```{r}
#| label: cluster
sce <- clusterGraph.se(sce, reddim.type = "MNN")
table(sce$clusters)
plotReducedDim(sce, "UMAP_MNN", colour_by = "clusters", text_by = "clusters")
```

### The number of neighbours is a resolution dial

With few neighbours, the graph is sparse and splits into many small
communities; with many neighbours, it forms fewer, larger ones:

```{r}
#| label: cluster-resolution
neighbours <- c(5, 10, 20, 50)
n_clusters <- sapply(neighbours, function(k) {
    sce_k <- clusterGraph.se(sce, reddim.type = "MNN", num.neighbors = k)
    length(unique(sce_k$clusters))
})
data.frame(neighbours, n_clusters)
```

There is no *correct* number of clusters, only the resolution at which the
biology you care about becomes visible. Clustering is a tool to generate
hypotheses, not a measurement: if two clusters have the same markers, merge
them; if a cluster obviously contains two cell types, split it.

### Are the clusters shared between donors?

```{r}
#| label: cluster-composition
composition <- table(cluster = sce$clusters, donor = sce$Donor)
composition
ggplot(as.data.frame(composition), aes(x = cluster, y = Freq, fill = donor)) +
    geom_col(position = "fill") +
    labs(x = "Cluster", y = "Proportion of cells") +
    theme_bw()
```

Most clusters gather cells from the three donors, but a few are dominated by
`Donor1`. A batch effect left over, or populations that are more abundant in
that donor? A cluster made of a single donor is suspect; one where the other
donors are present, but rarer, is more likely a difference in composition.
The markers will tell (@sec-markers).

## Marker genes {#sec-markers}

Clusters are numbers; biology needs names. Two complementary approaches:
check genes we already know, and ask the data which genes distinguish each
cluster.

### Known markers

@fig-testis lists genes that mark each cell type of the testis:

```{r}
#| label: panels
panels <- list(
    SSC            = c("UTF1", "ID4", "PIWIL4"),
    Spermatogonia  = c("DMRT1", "KIT", "MKI67"),
    Spermatocyte   = c("SYCP3", "DMC1", "SPO11"),
    RoundSpermatid = c("SUN5", "ACR", "BRDT"),
    ElongSpermatid = c("TNP1", "PRM1", "PRM2"),
    Sertoli        = c("SOX9", "AMH"),
    Leydig         = c("DLK1", "INHBA", "CYP17A1"),
    Myoid          = c("MYH11", "ACTA2"),
    Endothelial    = c("VWF", "PECAM1"),
    Macrophage     = c("CD14", "TYROBP")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: dotplot
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 9
plotDots(sce, features = unlist(panels), group = "clusters") +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

The size of a dot is the fraction of the cells of a cluster in which the gene
is detected; its colour, the average expression in the cluster. Read along each
cluster, and the names start writing themselves.

### Markers found by the data

`scoreMarkers.se()` compares each cluster with every other one, gene by gene,
and summarises the comparisons with **effect sizes**: Cohen's *d* (the
difference in mean expression, in units of standard deviation), the AUC (the
probability that a cell of the cluster expresses the gene more than a cell of
the other cluster), or the difference in the proportion of cells expressing it.
Blocking on the donor makes the comparisons within each donor.

```{r}
#| label: score-markers
markers <- scoreMarkers.se(sce, groups = sce$clusters, block = sce$Donor)
names(markers)
```

One table per cluster, with genes sorted by their average Cohen's *d* against
the other clusters. `previewMarkers()` shows the essential columns: the mean
expression in the cluster, the proportion of its cells expressing the gene, and
the average log-fold change with the other clusters.

```{r}
#| label: preview-markers
previewMarkers(markers[["1"]])
```

Plot the best marker of cluster 1 on the map:

```{r}
#| label: top-marker-umap
top_gene <- rownames(markers[["1"]])[1]
plotReducedDim(sce, "UMAP_MNN", colour_by = top_gene, text_by = "clusters")
```

:::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note icon='true'}

#### Question

Pick a cluster that looks somatic on the dot plot, and look at its top
markers. Do they agree with @fig-testis?

Why do we look at effect sizes, and not at p-values, to rank marker genes?

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

#### Answer

Replace `"1"` with the cluster of your choice, e.g. `previewMarkers(markers[["7"]])`.

The clusters were defined from these very expression values, precisely to
separate cells that differ. Testing whether they differ would be circular: the
p-values would all be tiny, and mean nothing. Effect sizes still rank genes by
how well they separate the clusters, which is all we need here.

:::
::::

## Annotation with a reference {#sec-annotation}

Annotating by hand does not scale, and only finds what you thought of looking
for. The alternative is to compare the cells with a **reference**: a dataset
whose cell types are already known.

`SingleR` [@aran2019] correlates each cell, or here each cluster, with the
profile of each cell type of the reference, using only genes that distinguish
the reference cell types, and keeps the best match. The workshop package
provides a reference built from the single-cell type atlas of the Human
Protein Atlas [@karlsson2021]: the average expression of each gene in
154 cell types from many tissues, the testis included.

```{r}
#| label: reference
HPA_ref <- GenE2scRNAseqIntro::HPA_ref
HPA_ref
head(sort(unique(HPA_ref$label)), 20)
```

With `clusters =`, `SingleR` first pools the cells of each cluster, and
labels the cluster as a whole: a pooled profile is much less noisy than a
single cell.

```{r}
#| label: singler
library(SingleR)
pred <- SingleR(
    test = sce,
    ref = HPA_ref,
    labels = HPA_ref$label,
    clusters = sce$clusters
)
pred[, c("labels", "pruned.labels")]
```

`pred` has one row per cluster. To give each **cell** the label of its
cluster, use a named vector as a lookup table:

```{r}
#| label: celltype
label_of_cluster <- setNames(pred$labels, rownames(pred))
sce$celltype <- label_of_cluster[as.character(sce$clusters)]
table(sce$celltype)
```

```{r}
#| label: umap-celltype
#| fig-width: 9
plotReducedDim(
    sce, "UMAP_MNN",
    colour_by = "celltype", text_by = "celltype", text_size = 3.5
)
```

Two things to observe on this map:

- The germ-cell labels line up along the differentiation path, in
  developmental order. Spermatogenesis is a **trajectory**, and clustering has
  cut it into segments whose boundaries depend on the resolution: do not
  over-interpret them.
- The somatic labels mark discrete populations: their boundaries are real.

:::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note icon='true'}

#### Question

In @sec-clustering, a few clusters were dominated by `Donor1`. Which cell types
are they?

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

#### Answer

```{r}
#| label: answer-celltype-donor
table(sce$celltype, sce$Donor)
```

`Donor1` contributes most of the spermatogonia and of the early spermatocytes.
The cells of the other donors are present in the same clusters, just rarer:
these samples differ in composition, which is biology (or sampling), not a
batch effect.

:::
::::

::: {.callout-warning icon='true'}

## A reference only knows what it contains

`SingleR` always returns the closest label, even when the right one is not in
the reference: check the labels against the markers. `pruned.labels` is `NA`
for the clusters whose best label barely beats the second best, which deserve
a second look.

:::

## Pseudobulk differential expression {#sec-pseudobulk}

### The unit of replication is the donor

We could compare two groups of **cells** directly, with thousands of cells per
group. But cells from the same donor are not independent observations: they
share a genome, a history and a sample preparation. Three donors are three
biological replicates, whether they gave 600 cells or 600,000. Tests that treat
each cell as a replicate give wildly over-confident p-values [@squair2021].

The standard solution is the **pseudobulk**: sum the counts of all the cells of
one cell type within one donor. This gives back a small, bulk-like matrix, with
one column per cell type and donor, which bulk RNA-seq tools such as `DESeq2`
[@love2014] analyse well. The two 10x runs of each donor are technical
replicates: they are summed too.

```{r}
#| label: pseudobulk
pb <- aggregateAcrossCells.se(
    sce,
    factors = colData(sce)[, c("celltype", "Donor")]
)
pb
head(colData(pb)[, c("factor.celltype", "factor.Donor", "counts")])
```

Each column of `pb` is one cell type in one donor; the `counts` column of
`colData(pb)` says how many cells were summed. Let's compare the two earliest
germ-cell populations: the spermatogonial stem cells (*undifferentiated
spermatogonia*) and the spermatogonia that have started to differentiate.

```{r}
#| label: pseudobulk-subset
spermatogonia <- c(
    "undifferentiated spermatogonia",
    "differentiating spermatogonia"
)
pb_sg <- pb[, pb$factor.celltype %in% spermatogonia]
samples <- data.frame(
    celltype = factor(pb_sg$factor.celltype, levels = spermatogonia),
    donor = pb_sg$factor.Donor,
    ncells = pb_sg$counts
)
samples
```

### Testing with `DESeq2`

::: {.callout-note icon='true'}

## `DESeq2` in a nutshell

`DESeq2` models the **raw counts** of each gene with a negative binomial
distribution, corrects for differences in library size with its own size
factors, and shares information across genes to estimate how variable each
gene is between replicates. The **design formula** describes the experiment:
`~ donor + celltype` compares the two cell types *within* each donor, which is
a paired design, and removes the differences between donors.

:::

```{r}
#| label: deseq
library(DESeq2)
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
    countData = assay(pb_sg, "sums"),
    colData = samples,
    design = ~ donor + celltype
)
dds <- dds[rowSums(counts(dds) >= 10) >= 3, ]
dds <- DESeq(dds)
res <- results(
    dds,
    contrast = c(
        "celltype",
        "differentiating spermatogonia",   # numerator
        "undifferentiated spermatogonia"   # denominator
    )
)
summary(res)
```

The first line keeps the genes with at least 10 counts in at least 3 of the 6
pseudo-samples. A positive log-fold change means a higher expression in the
differentiating spermatogonia. The most significant genes:

```{r}
#| label: deseq-top
res_df <- as.data.frame(res)
res_df <- res_df[order(res_df$padj), ]
head(res_df[, c("baseMean", "log2FoldChange", "padj")], 10)
```

Without being told anything, the test recovers the biology of the testis: the
stem-cell markers of @fig-testis are higher in the undifferentiated cells, and
genes of meiosis such as `SYCP3` are switched on in the differentiating ones.

```{r}
#| label: deseq-known
res_df[c("UTF1", "ID4", "PIWIL4", "SYCP3", "MKI67"), c("log2FoldChange", "padj")]
```

```{r}
#| label: volcano
res_df <- res_df[!is.na(res_df$padj), ]
ggplot(res_df, aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj), colour = padj < 0.05)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.8) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey70", `TRUE` = "firebrick")) +
    labs(
        x = "log2 fold change, differentiating / undifferentiated",
        y = "-log10(adjusted p-value)"
    ) +
    theme_bw()
```

::: {.callout-warning icon='true'}

## What this test can, and cannot, tell you

Our two groups were defined from the expression data, by clustering: they were
chosen to be different, so the p-values above are optimistic. Here, `DESeq2`
mostly helps rank genes.

Pseudobulk analyses shine when the groups are defined independently of the
expression data: comparing **conditions** (healthy *vs* infertile donors,
treated *vs* untreated...) **within one cell type**, with several donors per
condition. The code is exactly the same, with `~ condition` in the design.

:::

## Wrap-up {#sec-wrap-up}

### What we did

```{r}
#| label: recap
#| eval: false
# read the counts, and build the object
umi <- read.delim(umi_path, header = TRUE, row.names = 1)
counts_sparse <- Matrix(as.matrix(umi), sparse = TRUE)
sce <- SingleCellExperiment(assays = list(counts = counts_sparse))
split_names <- strsplit(colnames(sce), "\\.")
sce$Donor <- sapply(split_names, function(x) x[1])
sce$Replicate <- sapply(split_names, function(x) x[3])
sce$Sample <- paste(sce$Donor, sce$Replicate, sep = "_rep")
# quality control
is_mito <- grepl("^MT-", rownames(sce))
sce <- quickRnaQc.se(sce, subsets = list(Mito = is_mito), block = sce$Sample)
sce <- sce[, sce$keep]
# normalisation, feature selection, PCA
sce <- normalizeRnaCounts.se(sce, size.factors = sce$sum, block = sce$Sample)
sce <- chooseRnaHvgs.se(sce, block = sce$Sample, top = 2000)
sce <- runPca.se(sce, features = rowData(sce)$hvg, number = 25)
# batch correction, UMAP
sce <- correctMnn.se(sce, block = sce$Donor)
sce <- runUmap.se(sce, reddim.type = "MNN", output.name = "UMAP_MNN")
# clusters, markers, cell types
sce <- clusterGraph.se(sce, reddim.type = "MNN")
markers <- scoreMarkers.se(sce, groups = sce$clusters, block = sce$Donor)
pred <- SingleR(sce, ref = HPA_ref, labels = HPA_ref$label, clusters = sce$clusters)
sce$celltype <- setNames(pred$labels, rownames(pred))[as.character(sce$clusters)]
# pseudobulk
pb <- aggregateAcrossCells.se(sce, factors = colData(sce)[, c("celltype", "Donor")])
```

About twenty lines of code. Everything else was looking at the results and
deciding whether to believe them, which is the actual job.

### Where to go next

- The [`scrapbook`](https://bioconductor.org/books/release/scrapbook/) and
  [OSCA](https://bioconductor.org/books/release/OSCA/) books [@amezquita2020]
  explain each of these steps, and their alternatives, in depth.
- Spermatogenesis is a trajectory: *pseudotime* methods such as `TSCAN` or
  `slingshot` order the cells along it.
- For spatial transcriptomics, the
  [OSTA](https://bioconductor.org/books/release/OSTA/) book applies the same
  containers and many of the same steps to Visium and other technologies.

### Exercises

**1. Batch effects.** Cluster the cells on the **uncorrected** PCs, and redo
the composition plot of @sec-clustering. What changed?

:::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

#### Answer

```{r}
#| label: exercise-1
#| eval: false
sce$clusters_uncorrected <- clusterGraph.se(sce, reddim.type = "PCA")$clusters
composition <- table(cluster = sce$clusters_uncorrected, donor = sce$Donor)
ggplot(as.data.frame(composition), aes(x = cluster, y = Freq, fill = donor)) +
    geom_col(position = "fill")
```

Several clusters now contain cells of a single donor: without correction, part
of the clustering separates donors rather than cell types.

:::
::::

**2. Feature selection.** Redo the analysis with the top 500, then the top
5,000 HVGs, and compare the UMAPs. How sensitive is the picture to that choice?

:::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

#### Answer

```{r}
#| label: exercise-2
#| eval: false
sce_500 <- chooseRnaHvgs.se(sce, block = sce$Sample, top = 500)
sce_500 <- runPca.se(sce_500, features = rowData(sce_500)$hvg, number = 25)
sce_500 <- correctMnn.se(sce_500, block = sce_500$Donor)
sce_500 <- runUmap.se(sce_500, reddim.type = "MNN", output.name = "UMAP_MNN")
plotReducedDim(sce_500, "UMAP_MNN", colour_by = "celltype")
```

Then the same with `top = 5000`. The overall structure is robust; the fine
details of the map are not.

:::
::::

**3. Another reference.** Annotate the clusters with the *Human Primary Cell
Atlas*, a reference of purified cell types from the `celldex` package (it is
already downloaded in the workshop environment). Which populations does it
recognise, and what does it call the germ cells?

:::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

#### Answer

```{r}
#| label: exercise-3
#| eval: false
hpca <- celldex::HumanPrimaryCellAtlasData()
pred_hpca <- SingleR(
    test = sce, ref = hpca, labels = hpca$label.main, clusters = sce$clusters
)
data.frame(cluster = rownames(pred), HPA = pred$labels, HPCA = pred_hpca$labels)
```

The Human Primary Cell Atlas contains no germ cells: `SingleR` still gives them
the closest label it has. A reference can only recognise what it contains.

:::
::::

**4. Somatic cells.** Compare the Leydig cells with the peritubular myoid
cells, with a pseudobulk analysis. Which genes come up?

:::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

#### Answer

```{r}
#| label: exercise-4
#| eval: false
somatic <- c("leydig cells", "peritubular myoid cells")
pb_soma <- pb[, pb$factor.celltype %in% somatic]
samples_soma <- data.frame(
    celltype = factor(pb_soma$factor.celltype, levels = somatic),
    donor = pb_soma$factor.Donor
)
dds_soma <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
    countData = assay(pb_soma, "sums"),
    colData = samples_soma,
    design = ~ donor + celltype
)
dds_soma <- dds_soma[rowSums(counts(dds_soma) >= 10) >= 3, ]
dds_soma <- DESeq(dds_soma)
res_soma <- as.data.frame(results(dds_soma))
head(res_soma[order(res_soma$padj), ], 10)
```
